title: Kth Smallest Element in an Array
directAnswer: Don't sort the whole array — you only need one order statistic. A size-k max-heap gives the kth smallest in O(n log k). Quickselect does better: partition around a pivot (the same partition merge sort/quicksort uses), and recurse into only the side that contains target index k−1. That's O(n) average because work halves each step (n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n); worst case O(n²), fixed in practice by a random pivot.

remember.pattern: Quickselect — partition, then recurse into one side only
remember.formula:
target = k - 1                 # 0-indexed rank of kth smallest
lo, hi = 0, n - 1
while lo <= hi:
    p = partition(lo, hi)      # Lomuto: elements < pivot go left
    if p == target: return nums[p]
    elif p < target: lo = p + 1    # answer is to the RIGHT
    else: hi = p - 1               # answer is to the LEFT
rules: kth **smallest** maps to 0-indexed rank `target = k − 1`. The classic off-by-one is using `k` instead of `k − 1`.
Quickselect recurses into **one** side only — that's why it's O(n) average, not O(n log n). Recursing into both is just quicksort.
Lomuto partition returns the pivot's **final sorted position** `p`. Compare `p` to `target`: equal → done; `p < target` → go right; `p > target` → go left.
Worst case is O(n²) when the pivot is always extreme (already-sorted input). **Randomize the pivot** (swap a random index into `hi` before partitioning) to make that astronomically unlikely.

The heap baseline keeps a **max-heap of size k** — push, then pop the largest whenever size exceeds k. The top is the kth smallest. Use this when you want guaranteed O(n log k) with no worst-case blowup, or for a streaming input.
whenToUse: You need ONE order statistic (kth smallest/largest, median), not the full sorted order
The array is unsorted and you're allowed to mutate it (quickselect partitions in place)
Average-case O(n) matters and the data isn't adversarial
Streaming or memory-bounded: a size-k heap caps space at O(k)
antiSignals: You need the full sorted array anyway → just sort, O(n log n)
Many repeated kth queries on static data → sort once, answer each in O(1)
Worst-case guarantees are required and input may be adversarial → median-of-medians O(n) worst case, or the heap
You may not mutate the input and can't copy it → quickselect's in-place swaps are off the table
remember.takeaway: Selection is strictly easier than sorting: you only need the kth element, not all n in order. Quickselect reuses the partition primitive but throws away half the work each step, landing at O(n) average. The size-k heap is the safe, streaming-friendly O(n log k) fallback. Knowing both — and when each wins — is the interview signal.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you avoid the lazy sort-and-index answer and reach for selection, can implement partition correctly, and understand why recursing into one side gives O(n) average while the heap gives O(n log k).
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Off-by-one between k and k−1, recursing into both partition sides (turning quickselect back into quicksort), or claiming quickselect is O(n) worst case — it's O(n²) without a random pivot.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Offer the heap baseline first for its clean O(n log k) guarantee, then present quickselect for O(n) average, and proactively mention the random-pivot fix and the median-of-medians O(n) worst-case option.

problemStatement:
Given an integer array `nums` and an integer `k`, return the **kth smallest** element in the array.

Note that it is the kth smallest element in sorted order, **not** the kth distinct element — duplicates count toward the rank.
constraints: Duplicates are allowed and count toward the rank
understanding: Find the element that would sit at 0-indexed position k−1 if the array were sorted ascending. You don't need the rest of the order — just that one slot. Duplicates are real elements: in [3, 3, 3] the 2nd smallest is 3.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is k 1-indexed?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — k = 1 means the minimum. In code that's the element at 0-indexed position k − 1, so converting to target = k − 1 up front avoids off-by-one bugs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: kth smallest counting duplicates, or kth distinct value?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Counting duplicates. In [1, 2, 2, 3] the 3rd smallest is 2, not 3. If they wanted distinct values, dedupe first.

clarifyingQuestions.question: May I rearrange the array?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Confirm this. Quickselect partitions in place and reorders elements. If the caller needs the original order, copy first or use the heap.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What if the input could be adversarial / already sorted?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Then plain quickselect can hit O(n²). Randomize the pivot, or use the heap for a hard O(n log k) guarantee.

examples.explanation: Duplicates count toward the rank — every order statistic here is 2.

approaches.name: Max-Heap of Size k — Baseline
approaches.whenToMention: Offer this first as the clean, safe answer with a hard O(n log k) bound — great for streams and when you can't risk quickselect's worst case.
hints: If you keep only the k smallest elements seen so far, the largest among them is the kth smallest overall. What structure gives you the current largest in O(1) and removes it in O(log k)?
Use a max-heap capped at size k. Push each element; if the heap grows past k, pop the largest. The heap always holds the k smallest seen.
After processing every element, the heap's top (its maximum) is exactly the kth smallest of the whole array.
approaches.complexityReasoning: n pushes, each O(log k) on a heap of size ≤ k, and at most n pops of O(log k) → O(n log k) time. The heap never exceeds k elements → O(k) space.
approaches.explanation:
Reframe 'kth smallest' as 'the largest of the k smallest'. If you could hold onto just the k smallest elements you've seen, then the biggest of those k *is* the kth smallest once you've seen everything.

**Why a max-heap and not a min-heap.** You want O(1) access to the *largest* of your current k keepers, because that's the candidate most likely to be evicted when a smaller element arrives. A max-heap puts that largest at the top. Push each new element; if the heap now holds `k + 1` elements, pop the top (the largest) — it can't be among the k smallest. After the full pass, the heap contains exactly the k smallest elements and its top is the kth smallest.

**Why the size cap makes this efficient.** Every heap operation costs `O(log(size))`, and the size is bounded by `k`, not `n`. So even though you touch all `n` elements, each costs `O(log k)`. When `k` is small relative to `n`, `O(n log k)` is a real win over the `O(n log n)` of sorting — and it never degrades, unlike quickselect.

**Why this shines on streams.** You never need all `n` elements in memory at once — only the current `k` keepers. That makes the heap the natural choice when data arrives incrementally or when `O(k)` space is the constraint. The trade is the `log k` factor on every element; quickselect drops that on average but demands the whole array up front and mutates it.

**Symmetry note.** For kth *largest* you'd flip to a min-heap of size k; the top would then be the kth largest. Same idea, mirrored comparator.
approaches.insight: The size-k heap is the 'keep the best k seen so far' pattern — the same engine behind Top K Frequent Elements and K Closest Points. The trick is choosing the heap orientation opposite to what you're selecting: a *max*-heap to find a *smallest*, so the easiest element to discard sits at the top.

dryRun.intro: Max-heap capped at size 3. Push each element; pop the largest whenever size exceeds 3. Top at the end is the 3rd smallest.

java.explanation: Max-heap: the largest keeper sits on top, ready to be evicted.
Cap the heap at k so every op is O(log k), not O(log n).
Remove the largest — it can't belong to the k smallest.
After the pass, the top of the size-k max-heap is the kth smallest.

python.explanation: Python's heapq is a min-heap; storing negatives turns it into a max-heap.
Push the negation so the largest x is the smallest stored value (top).
Pops the most-negative entry = the largest x → evict it.
Negate the top to recover the kth smallest actual value.

pitfalls: Using a min-heap by reflex — then the top is the smallest, not the kth smallest.
Forgetting the size cap — the heap grows to n and you've just sorted in O(n log n).
In Python, forgetting to negate on the way out — returns -value.

approaches.name: Quickselect — Partition and Recurse One Side (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer interviewers push toward for O(n) average. Lead with 'it's quicksort's partition, but I only recurse into the side that holds my target'.
hints: Quicksort's partition places one pivot into its final sorted position p and splits the rest into < pivot and ≥ pivot. If p equals your target index, you're done — for free.
If p < target, the kth smallest is in the right part; if p > target, it's in the left part. Recurse (or loop) into only that side — never both.
Convert k to a 0-indexed target = k - 1. Average work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = O(n). Guard the O(n²) worst case with a random pivot.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each partition is O(size). On average a pivot splits roughly in half, so total work is n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n = O(n). Adversarial input that always picks an extreme pivot degrades to n + (n−1) + … = O(n²); a random pivot makes that effectively impossible. Iterative loop uses O(1) extra space.
approaches.explanation:
Quickselect is quicksort with a shortcut: since you only want the element at one position, you discard the half that can't contain it.

**The partition primitive (Lomuto).** Pick a pivot (here `nums[hi]`). Sweep `j` from `lo` to `hi−1`, maintaining a boundary `i`: every element strictly less than the pivot is swapped to the left of `i`, and `i` advances. After the sweep, swap the pivot into position `i`. Now `nums[i]` is in its **final sorted position** — everything left of it is smaller, everything right is ≥. That returned index `p = i` is the pivot's true rank.

**The shortcut that beats sorting.** Compare `p` to `target = k − 1`. If `p == target`, the pivot is the kth smallest — return it immediately, no further work. If `p < target`, the kth smallest lies strictly to the right, so set `lo = p + 1` and repeat on the right segment only. If `p > target`, it lies to the left, so set `hi = p − 1`. Crucially you recurse into **one** side. Quicksort recurses into both (that's why it's `O(n log n)`); throwing away one side is what collapses the average cost to `O(n)`.

**Why O(n) average but O(n²) worst.** A balanced pivot halves the remaining range, so the work telescopes: `n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n`. But if the pivot is always the max or min — which happens on already-sorted input with last-element pivots — each step shrinks the range by just one, giving `n + (n−1) + … + 1 = O(n²)`. The standard fix is a **random pivot**: before partitioning, swap a uniformly random index into `hi`. An adversary can no longer force bad splits, so the expected time is `O(n)` regardless of input order. For a hard worst-case guarantee, median-of-medians picks a provably good pivot in `O(n)`, yielding `O(n)` worst case at the cost of a larger constant.

**The off-by-one and over-recursion traps.** (1) Using `k` instead of `k − 1` for the target returns the element one slot off. (2) Recursing into both sides quietly turns this into quicksort — same answer, worse complexity. (3) Comparing with `<` vs `<=` inside partition affects how duplicates land but not correctness of the selected rank; keep it consistent. Say the invariant aloud — 'after partition, p is the pivot's final rank; I keep only the side containing target' — and the logic stays tight.
approaches.insight: The whole speedup is one decision: recurse into a single side. Sorting answers 'what is every element's rank?'; selection answers only 'what sits at rank k?' — a strictly smaller question, so it admits a strictly cheaper algorithm. That 'solve exactly what's asked, not more' instinct generalizes: binary search, two pointers, and quickselect all win by refusing to compute order they don't need.

pitfalls: Using k instead of k − 1 as the target index — returns the wrong rank.
Recursing into both sides — that's quicksort, O(n log n), not quickselect.
Claiming O(n) worst case — it's O(n²) without a random pivot on sorted input.
Forgetting the final pivot swap in partition — the returned index isn't the pivot's true rank.

edgeCases.behavior: Single element; target = 0, first partition returns p = 0 = target → returns 5.
All duplicates; any pivot lands somewhere, but every value is 2 → returns 2 regardless of split.
The random pivot prevents the O(n²) degeneration that a fixed last-element pivot would suffer here.

commonMistakes: Off-by-one: targeting index k instead of k − 1.
Recursing into both partition sides — collapses quickselect into quicksort.
Using a min-heap instead of a max-heap for the size-k baseline.
Claiming quickselect is O(n) worst case — it's O(n²) without pivot randomization.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: k vs k − 1 off-by-one
commonMistakesDetailed.why: kth smallest is 1-indexed but arrays are 0-indexed. Targeting index k returns the (k+1)th smallest.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
int target = k;            // WRONG: off by one
if (p == target) return nums[p];
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
int target = k - 1;        // 0-indexed rank
if (p == target) return nums[p];

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Recursing into both sides
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Quickselect's speed comes from discarding the half that can't hold the target. Recursing into both is just quicksort — O(n log n), not O(n) average.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
p = self._partition(nums, lo, hi)
self.select(nums, lo, p - 1, target)   # WRONG: also recurses left
self.select(nums, p + 1, hi, target)   # and right

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Fixed pivot on sorted input
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Always picking the last element as pivot makes already-sorted input degrade to O(n²) — every partition peels off just one element.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad: int pivot = nums[hi];      // fixed pivot → O(n^2) on sorted input

patternNote: Canonical Quickselect (order statistics). Trigger whenever you need a single kth smallest/largest from an unsorted, mutable array and want O(n) average. Reuse the quicksort partition but recurse into one side only. The size-k heap is the O(n log k) streaming-safe fallback; median-of-medians is the O(n) worst-case variant.
